messages.author: 52e7d58571bf053d
messages.subject: SEM
parts:
Dear group,

After doing a structural equation model with the SEM package of R, I get these results: chi squared=5.10, gl=5, p=0.40; CFI=1.000, TLI=0.99, and RMSEA=0.009; 95% CI=0.000-0.09.

why could it be that you get that CFI=1? Is it a problem that there is a perfect fit?
Thanks in advance.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: SEM
parts: why could it be that you get that CFI=1?

It happens whenever chi-squared < its degrees of freedom, or not substantially > its df (so that it is merely 1 after rounding).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: SEM
parts:
You don't have perfect fit, or chi-square would be zero (and so would RMSEA).

CFI isn't 1.0000000000 [etc], it's rounded to two decimals. What was your null chi-square?

Jeremy

messages.author: 5b9c62b1c7cbc1e6
messages.subject: Re: SEM
parts:
Then you're in the delicate position of having to educate the reviewer (wait until they find out TLI can be >1). It just means your model fits very well.

Even if you had a saturated model (chi-square = 0, df = 0, and CFI would be exactly 1), that would not mean there was anything 'wrong.' It would mean your model is not falsifiable, but if the model is correctly specified, the parameter estimates would still be correct.

Good luck
Pat
